utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody and good afternoon to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci madam. Prosecution today is represented by Mr. Thayer. Absent amongst the Defence teams is Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Petrusic and Mr. Haynes and Mr. Josse. No. Mr. Josse is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm here today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You are easily provoked Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was my fault, I had my hand covering my face. I was trying to be extremely anonymous and quiet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So the witness is present. We are going -- good afternoon to you, Mr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to finish with your testimony today. Is that correct, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Then you can proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Likewise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Based on what you told us yesterday, I wanted to follow up on a couple of points, and to do that I just want to review with you some of the things you said yesterday and make sure that we have your best recollection of some of these events. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday Mr. Bourgon asked you the followed question, and this is page 26508, referring to Colonel Lazic: "Question: To your knowledge, sir, did this colonel have the authority to order you to fire the guns of the Bratunac Brigade?" And your answer was: "He arrived with an order. He had been ordered by someone from the corps that the artillery be used. That is for certain." And then I asked you the following question, and this was at page 26535: "Question: Now, you testified earlier today that Colonel Lazic arrived with an order, and I just want to clarify that with you. Is it your testimony that he arrived in person with an order?" And your answer was: "Colonel Lazic came personally to the brigade command. This is why I was trying to remember how that tallied with his arrival. It is certain that on that day when my report was drafted, there was a report sent to the brigade command and I presume he arrived there personally conveying someone else's order from the corps command. Either that, or in the meantime, he was in contact with someone from the corps but I had no insight into that." And just to complete this portion of your testimony, you testified a little while later at page 26540: "Now, I just realised when I rewound the whole film, he probably arrived to actually hand over the duties in the Bratunac Brigade on that day." And then you repeated four pages days later: "I believe that day Colonel Lazic on behalf of the Drina Corps and carried out the changeover of the brigade commanders." Let me just give you a couple of moments to let the interpretation catch up and let that sink in.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly, sir, that it was only yesterday that you recalled for the first time that Colonel Lazic was present in the Bratunac Brigade on 25 May 1995 because of the changeover ceremony?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state for sure that Colonel Lazic on that day arrived in Bratunac. Yesterday, when I told you that I recalled that on the 25th of May 1995 Colonel Blagojevic received his duty, in keeping with that, it is for that reason that he was there since someone on behalf of the command had to be present during the changeover between the commanders. Therefore, I think, although I don't know it for certain, that on that day Colonel Lazic was also the Bratunac Brigade commander since the brigade was in between commanders at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's explore that a little bit, sir. The shells that your brigade fired at the safe area were fired at approximately 7.00 p.m. in the evening, 1907 hours to be specific. Right? I can show you the report if you don't remember that time.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that yesterday in the report, but I can't recall it off the cuff without the report, although I reread the report twice yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's have P216 on e-court, please. Sir, you've raised this issue of the handover, so I want to follow up on that with you. And if I may have the assistance of Madam Usher, I can the e-court version may be somewhat illegible so I would the witness to have the original version. Sir, I'm handing you the handwritten original copy that was drafted by Colonel Blagojevic of this document, as well as the typewritten version of it that went out. Just ask you to take a look at that. We can see on the e-court in paragraph 2 the print is a little washed out, that's why I wanted you to be able to look at the original. Do you see paragraph 2? It might be easier to read the typewritten version, sir. We have paragraph 1: "The enemy did not conduct combat operations against our forces." And in paragraph 2: "Our forces did not open fire towards the demilitarised zone." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then do you see where it says at 1000 hours, that's 10.00 in the morning; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "The transfer of duties of commander of the 1st Bratunac Light Brigade was carried out in the presence of the Drina Corps commander Major General Zivanovic and the president of the Bratunac municipal assembly Mr. Simic." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So we can clearly see it was General Zivanovic who was there from the corps; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me about things I did not need to know and I can only repeat my answer when I was examined by Mr. Bourgon. He asked me what were the duties of chief of artillery. I said then that it is a staff officer who in all aspects is subordinated to the brigade commander, merely assisting the commander when commanding his artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, well, let me just ask you, do you have any reason to doubt the accuracy of that daily combat report that General Zivanovic was there at 10.00 in the morning for the handover?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need for me to argue either way. As the chief of artillery, it wasn't up to me to follow who was there, who was leaving, who kept notes and who was reporting. It was someone else's duty in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We are done with that document. And again we see that that was sent out at about 4.30 in the afternoon. Now, again, your howitzers fired those shots at 7 minutes after 7.00 that meaning. I'm going to ask you, sir -- do you want to see the report for the time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. 1907 hours, your howitzers fired those shells. My question to you, sir, is, do you think that if Colonel Lazic in fact were there, do you think he was hanging around the Bratunac Brigade command for nine hours after the changeover ceremony or do you think your memory might be mistaken about him physically being at the brigade headquarters at that time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose you don't think I came here to make up things.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I would just ask you to please answer the question that I put to you.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anything of it. I have no opinion about it. I was engaged in my duties. The rest was with some other people who may have been tasked to follow at what time Lazic arrived and where he went. It wasn't part of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let me share with you a little bit about what Colonel Lazic told this Trial Chamber about this order. This is at page 21858 to 59 of the transcript. He said: "I did not have the right to order, to issue orders, and this is evident. I was not an organ who could issue orders. How come I mention -- my name is mentioned with regard to this order given the fact that both of them were professional officers and knew very well that they were not supposed to receive orders from somebody who did not have the right to issue orders. How and what happened in the operations room and how the duty operations officer passed on the order referring to me and mentioning my name, I really wouldn't know. I only know that I did not have the right to issue this order." I then asked Colonel Lazic if he would have been in a position to pass on as opposed to issuing that order and he replied, this is at page 21860: "I've said it that I cannot remember such a possibility although I'm not ruling it out. I'm not ruling this out but I'm saying that I can't remember having passed this order personally on. I may have been in the operations room when the duty officer was passing on this order and he may have said something to the effect, 'here you have Colonel Lazic here, so execute the order.' That may have happened but I don't have any recollection of that and that's why my answer was what it was." So bear with me, sir, I just need to complete some of this testimony from Colonel Lazic so you understand where I'm coming from when I put the question to you. I then asked Colonel Lazic." Just as a points of clarification, Colonel, as a matter of how the VRS and organised armies operate, isn't it the case that simply as chief of operations and training you would have been in a position to pass on such an order from your superior command to the Bratunac Brigade? " And his answer was: "I personally believe that if the Main Staff had issued an order to this effect, then the order was passed either to the commander or the Chief of Staff. I don't believe that somebody would have looked for me to communicate the order to me and to ask for me to pass it on. That's why I'm saying that it is possible that I was in the operations room and that the duty officer said something to the effect, here, Milenko Lazic is here and that's why my name is mentioned because the two senior reporting officers had to mention somebody who could have passed on the order. And I personally say and I repeat, I don't know how this could have occurred because I had not issued the order."

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I could tell from the document it is the 25th of May at 7.10 and I believe it was forwarded at 8.10. Do you think that at that point in time we could have been contemplating the situation nowadays and firing at someone we should not have. I stand by what I said that Colonel Lazic was at the Bratunac Brigade command, and I heard that it was on his orders that fire should be opened. Whether that stemmed from the corps command or whether it came from him personally, I can't say. Since I wrote that down and since my commander wrote it down and it was his first day on duty, it must be true. I don't think he would have been crazy enough to write things down that did not actually take place, and fire at things he shouldn't have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you just said that "I heard that it was on his orders that fire should be opened." Who did you hear that from, sir, and when?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been his order to the brigade commander, but I can't recall such details. I'm sorry, I recall many things but I would have shared this had I remembered it. It is a bit hazy and therefore I can't deny or confirm things I'm not 100 percent sure of. What I am sure of, however, I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just make sure that the record is clear. Is it your testimony that you don't remember who gave you the order to fire those shells on the safe area?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't remember whether I ordered this to the unit or whether it was ordered by the brigade commander himself. That little piece of information is missing from my memory. Therefore I can't argue in favour of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to follow-up now on some questions which Mr. Karnavas put to you during your Blagojevic testimony, after the Prosecution had shown you the two reports that we are talking about. And he read to you an excerpt from a Dutch organisation's report about what was going on that day to see if that might jog your recollection as to why Colonel Lazic may have ordered you to shell Srebrenica. This was at the transcript page 8609 of the Blagojevic trial. And this is what he read to you: "Much of the Bosnian/Serb revenge following the NATO bombing of Pale on 25 and 26 May concentrated on Sarajevo. But the eastern enclaves were not spared. This also had repercussions on the situation around Srebrenica. On 25 May, as immediate retaliation, a number of shells landed close to a school in Srebrenica. There were one dead and three wounded. The VRS also opened fire on the southwestern part of the enclave." Now, sir, Mr. Kar navas put the question to you: "According to the report there was a retaliation. Does this now cause you to recollect why you might have been ordered by Colonel Lazic to fire the artillery as you so indicate in your report?" Your answer was: "I can't recall. I really can't recall that detail. I'm sure we fired. I know we were targeted that day from a tank and that we returned anti-armour fire. One of our artillery pieces was destroyed. Some of my men were injured, but I'm sorry, I really can't remember. I don't know." Now, sir, you've managed to recall some details as you sat here yesterday, some new details, so I want to know first of all if you stand by the answer I just read back to you or whether your recollection has changed regarding the events that Mr. Karnavas recited to you.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer stands, the same way I answered Mr. Karnavas. I don't recall. I do remember that there was an accident, that three of my men were injured and the piece was destroyed. I know our firing position was targeted. As for the rest, I don't remember and I can't state anything I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's see if we can refresh or jog your recollection a little bit about the events of that day, what was going on in the brigade and what your particular activities were. Can we have 65 ter 3359, please. Okay. Sir, do you see the document in front of you, nothing new, same document we've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the first paragraph obviously we discussed yesterday. I want to turn your attention to paragraphs 2 through 4 of this document. Paragraph 2 indicates that brigade units are ordered to be in full combat readiness. Work obligation battalion is mobilised and is ready for engagement. Then it lists where the brigade commanding officers are. One of them is at the command post and some of them are with subordinate units. It refers to measures being taken pursuant to an order in paragraph 3, and in paragraph 4 it states that the brigade command monitors the situation and is ready to carry out combat activities with its units as situation develops. Do you see all that there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, it's clear from this document, sir, is it not, that something significant has occurred to place the brigade on full combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I remember the day vaguely. What happened happened and for me it was a grave moment, and I'm really not able to remember any further details of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this interim combat report went out at 9.10 in the evening. The regular combat report that we looked at a few moments ago when out at about 4.30 in the afternoon, and if you recall, it listed everything as relatively normal or what passes for normal during wartime. The enemy did not conduct combat operations against our forces, our forces did not open fire towards the demilitarised zone. You remember that language from the regular combat report; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost every combat report contained that. Regular combat reports were sent during that period and as I say, this is an interim combat report which was sent because something must have certainly happened after that time. Otherwise, this interim combat report would not have been drafted in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's exactly my point, sir. Something happened between 4.30 and about 9.00 p.m. that night when that interim combat report was issued. Now, there's an order that's referred to at paragraph 3, and I don't suppose you recall just by looking at that and looking back in time what that order was about, do you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order is an order of a superior command, and it was not for my eyes. It was for other people, the security officer, the commander, some other people were supposed to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at 65 ter 3370. You see the document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please take a moment and read it. With Madam Usher's assistance, I'd also like to show you the original because as we can see on the e-court version, the time stamp has been smudged out. Now, sir, have you had a chance to read the document?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. What we have here is an order dated 25 May 1995 from General Zivanovic, and if you could just look at the time stamp and indicate when that was received and processed?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is in the evening, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was processed in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this document indicates that today at 1558 hours, the forces of the NATO pact have carried out a fire attack against the Jahorinski Potok warehouse and it indicates that General Zivanovic wants to raise the units of the Drina Corps to the highest level of combat readiness. You see that, sir, in paragraph 1 of the order?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And he says the opening of fire shall be regulated by the Drina Corps through the Grabovica signals table. My first question to you, sir, is what is the Grabovica signals table, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this order before, so I would not be able to tell you the meaning of this Grabovica signals table.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the last line of the order, it refers to implementing the relocation of the artillery from the basic firing positions to reserve firing positions and turning the basic firing positions into decoy ones. And this we can see was in fact distributed to your brigade as well, sir. Now, you are telling the Court that you don't remember seeing this order. My question is, do you recall taking any steps that would be consistent with responding to this order from General Zivanovic? For example, relocating the artillery in your brigade.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at one point an order was issued to make up decoy firing positions, which we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you another document. It's 65 ter 3788, sir. And I want you to please take a moment and read this document. When you've had a chance to read it, including the order, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he is ready.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm done reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we have here another order from General Zivanovic, again dated 25 May 1995. And if we can scroll to the top of the page of the B/C/S, do you see where it says that it was received on May 26th at 20 minutes after midnight?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 26 May, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, this document states that the NATO aircraft fired on the facilities of the VRS and that the VRS responded accordingly with activities against the selected targets. If we move to the order, if you look at paragraph 2 it states: "In case the UNPROFOR forces continue with the activities against our military targets and civilian targets, all corps units have to be in readiness to fire at UNPROFOR checkpoints and bases." And if we go down to paragraph 4, referring to the anti-aircraft assets, "open fire at the UNPROFOR aircrafts pursuant to the authorisation of the VRS Main Staff..." My question again to you, sir, is does reading this order refresh your recollection at all about the events of 25 May and any actions you took as chief of artillery of the Bratunac Brigade in response to those actions and in response to this order?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just told you these combat orders that arrived from the corps commander were taken to the brigade command directly. These combat reports never reached me. There was no need for them to reach me. Everything that was ordered within the framework of the brigade, what the brigade commander ordered us, we were supposed to implement. And I'm telling you again that I had men injured, men in hospital, and it's very hard for me to remember any such details. Those were difficult times for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we may have 3D506 on e-court, please. I want to show you one more document in connection with this topic. This is a regular combat report from the Bratunac Brigade dated 26 May 1995. And we have this language, do you see at paragraph 1: "Enemy forces did not carry out any combat activities or provocative actions against our positions." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see paragraph 2: "Combat readiness of our units complies with measures ordered by the superior command." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, there's no mention of any tank firing from Budak at your artillery firing position, is there?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report for the 26th of May, and what you are talking about happened on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. My first question to you is do you see anything here on the 26th, considering this was the day after a very busy day for you, do you see anything in this report referring to any tank fire being levelled at your firing position? There's nothing in there, is there, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you reply to the question, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know what the basis for this question is. I did not hear any evidence from the witness about fire being opened on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Thayer? Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the question I've just put to the witness. I think the purpose of my question is quite clear. I think the witness himself just stated that this has to do with the 26th and the firing that he was talking about occurred on the 25th. And I'm just trying to establish that there is nothing in the report for the day after concerning any firing by any tank just in case it didn't make it into the report on the 25th, which I think the witness will agree also contains no reference to a tank firing on the brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, there is a limit which you shouldn't exceed and you've just exceeded it now. You should have stopped at the end of the previous sentence. Let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We believe that this point has been belaboured a little bit too much. We don't really see the point of pressing with this question unless you insist, Mr. Thayer --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and unless it was a stepping stone for your next question or the one after. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It was my last question on this topic and so I'm prepared to move on absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then I think you can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to turn your attention to the Krivaja-95 operation. Your brigade no doubt received the warning order and the order for active combat operations from the corps both dated 2 July 1995 signed by General Zivanovic. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All combat orders from the corps came to the brigade commander rather than to the chief of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then, certainly the relevant portions of those orders would be communicated to you as chief of artillery; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was regular briefing by the brigade commander and if I was present at those regular briefings, I know that at a certain point in time the commander went to Vlasenici and I didn't know anything further until the 5th in the evening or the 6th in the morning. I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just look at a couple of documents very quickly, I just want to ask you a couple of questions. May we have 65 ter 106, please. Sir, this is the warning order from the corps regarding Krivaja-95. If we go to page 2 of the original document, paragraph F, there's a reference to the 5th MAP shall detach all types of artillery weapons that will be engaged in support of the forces carrying out active combat operations. My only question about this document to you, sir, is what it the 5th MAP?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the mixed artillery regiment which was on the strength of the Drina Corps. To be more precise, it was attached to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we may have 65 ter 107, please. Sir, what we have here is the order for active combat operations Krivaja-95 from the corps. If we can go to page 4 of the B/C/S, please, and it's page 5 of the English. Sir, can you see at number 6 under "artillery support" it refers to composition of KAG. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps artillery group.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is that and what was it composed of?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All units engaged in operations had the necessary fire support. The Bratunac Brigade, i.e., the brigade artillery group did not have to and indeed did not provide any artillery support to these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, do you know what the composition of the Drina Corps, the KAG was?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were engaged in operations, you mean? I don't know. I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, there's a reference here to during preparatory fire to neutralise the enemy targets as per plan for preparatory fire, and there are numerous references throughout this combat order to the artillery plan. My question to you, sir, is did you ever review that artillery plan for this operation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days ago I saw that plan for the first time, if you are referring to this plan under the name Susica, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you, sir, with respect to the plan Krivaja-95 do you ever recall seeing the artillery plan for that operation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you really think that Krivaja was lowered at such a low level that all of us officers in the brigade were actually aware of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My question was simple, sir. Just yes or no. Did you see the plan or --

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, may we have 65 ter 108, please. We have here, if you can look at the document on your screen, sir, an anti-aircraft order in connection with this operation dated 5 July 1995. If you look at paragraph 4, do you see the reference to deploying S-2M missiles and there's a specific reference to your brigade. Do you see that reference it's subpart A, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It says: One S-2 and detachment to be deployed in the Zagoni-Kokarda area to defend the town of Bratunac and the forces operating with within the range of the S-2 Ms. First of all, what is an S-2M?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me tell you this. This is an order for anti-aircraft Defence. I was the chief of land artillery, not the anti-aircraft artillery. And S-2M are devices for anti-aircraft defence which had crews of two soldiers. That, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, where is this area of Zagoni-Kokarda, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the area that extends along the defence line of Bratunac. I don't know where exactly they were deployed, but it should with been an elevated point because they had to be independent. I don't know exactly where they were, but I can suppose that they were somewhere around there in that part of the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, you have told the Trial Chamber that you didn't receive these orders yourself. Now, there was immediately a lot of command staff work at your brigade to prepare for these active combat operations; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all surprised when this order arrived and when the operation started.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we may have 65 ter 219, please. And we will need page 9 of both the B/C/S and the English. Now, sir, as you may have seen when we flashed up the cover of this document, it's the reports and meetings of the Bratunac Brigade. You are familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you already that the first time I learned of the operation of the attack on Srebrenica on the 5th in the afternoon or the 6th in the morning. Here it says that the working meeting was on the 5th of July, so this is what I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Right, sir, and if we go back just that one day to the 4th of July, do you see the "Chief of Staff read the order from the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps for full combat readiness of our unit," do you see that? That's the first line for the entry for 4 July.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, were you present for these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you just referred to the 5th of July entry where it indicates the "Chief of Staff will go to the 1st Infantry Battalion to increase the accuracy and direction of artillery fire." Do you remember that happening, sir, in preparation for the Krivaja-95 operation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know about the operation is that we were in the brigade commander's office, we were summoned there and he issued tasks to us. He said that all chiefs and assistant commanders should draft proposals in order to have an order issued about the attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that in a moment, sir, because I think you've testified previously that you did present proposals to your commander. But my question was, do you remember the Chief of Staff going to the 1st Infantry Battalion to increase the accuracy and the direction of the artillery fire, do you remember that happening as chief of artillery?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Each battalion had its own battalion artillery support, this being a 120 or 82 millimetre mortar platoon. It was under the command of the brigade commander rather than chief of artillery per establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at another document, 65 ter 987, please. Now, there's a typewritten version but we can work with the handwritten version. Do you see the reference on this daily combat report dated July 4, 1995, sir, that the brigade commander is visiting the artillery firing positions?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite customary during our regular activities for a certain officer to visit the positions made from the command of the Drina Corps or another staff. They visit the units and control their combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forgiven. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't mind a musical accompaniment from time to time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends on who the composer is, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I understand you are just telling us it's customary. My specific question is, do you recall whether your brigade commander visited your, for example, firing position since you were not only artillery chief but you were also the commander of a unit, do you remember Commander Blagojevic visiting your position prior to the commencement of operation Krivaja-95?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the changeover on the 25th of May, Blagojevic of course visited all of his units acquainting himself with the forward lines and the rest. I recall that on a day, I don't know which precisely, that he came to visit, we toured our firing positions and wanted to know what the equipment was that we had at our disposal in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at 65 ter -- actually it's P03025, please. Sir, this is the Bratunac Brigade order for active combat operations Krivaja-95 operational order number 1. You've seen this before, clearly; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You testified in Blagojevic that you personally received the document and that you were duty-bound to sign for it and to read it. You can confirm that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you just told us that you made some proposals in connection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd just like a reference, I'm trying to follow in the testimony from the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Thayer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sure. That was 8478 of the transcript in Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to page 4 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. Do you see at number 6 under "fire support"?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the reference to the BrAG, that's the brigade's mixed artillery group; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you testified yesterday as to the composition and size of those weapons and where they were deployed; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, there's a reference here to the basic firing position according to current deployment and plan. Do you see that under 6.1, sir? Can you just read out what it says under 6.1?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Brigade artillery group consisting of a 105 millimetre howitzer platoon, a 122 millimetre gun platoon, and a B1 gun battery. Basic firing positions. According to current disposition ..." should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's fine for now, sir, thank you. Now, what kinds of artillery pieces did the battalion batteries have?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no battalion batteries. They have mortar platoons the calibre of which is either 82 or 120 millimetres. Depending on the manning strength of the battalion, these may not be platoons but squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, each of those platoons or squads within the battalion had their own komandirs or commanding officers; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, squad commander subordinated to the company commander who in turn is subordinated to the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you testified in Blagojevic that, and I quote, this is from 8539: "When it comes to major operations such as this one," and you were referring to Krivaja-95, "the chief of artillery must be directly superior to his subordinates, that is the commanding officers of the units, et cetera, down the line, down the chain of command." And that would refer to those individual units; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So your testimony is that they were not subordinate to you in any fashion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not subordinated to me. They were subordinated to the commander of the infantry battalion. His unit, his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, when you testified in Blagojevic then, what were you referring to in terms of you exercising superior command over subordinates, that is the commanding officers of the units down the line, down the chain of command, what did you mean then when you were testifying in Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I commanded platoon and battery commanders within the brigade artillery group. I did not command the mortar units. As per establishment, they are not part of the artillery group that was subordinated to me. They fell under battalion commanders, infantry battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about the 128 millimetre rocket launcher platoon, was that under your command, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of such a platoon in our unit. I know there was a rocket launcher of 57 millimetre. It was a makeshift device serving psychological purposes rather than being an efficient weapon. It was not much of an artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, do you remember testifying in Blagojevic, and this is at page 8493 of the transcript: "Question: And were you in charge of that rocket platoon in light of your position as the commander of artillery?" And you answered to Mr. Karnavas: "Yes." Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. But in the combat order drafted by Colonel Blagojevic it says first fire should be opened and then that unit was supposed to move under my authority. It is on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So the question is simple, sir, you were in command of that platoon; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That unit was attached to me for the purpose of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see that it's 3.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The break would be at quarter to 4.00. If you wish to break now, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll work with one more document, Mr. President. I didn't know if there was some special time today as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, quarter to 4:00. Yes, Mr. Bourgon, is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd just like to address the Court before the break in respect of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, in his absence I suppose, no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In that case perhaps we can let the witness go and we can discuss it now before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, I prefer to let my colleague go, Mr. President. I don't want to interrupt anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very sensitive, Mr. Bourgon. Let's have your next question or questions on the other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm being serenaded with music and sensitivity. I'll get flowers next, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, next you will be exchanging bouquets of flowers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, if we may take a look at P03785. And if we could move the image down to the lower left. In other words, if we could below up the upper right-hand portion a little bit. Sir, do you see the image in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see two firing positions. Three, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you have a hard time with the resolution of the image, I have a hard copy here that you can look at and refer to, but if you are okay with that. What I'd like you to do is just take the little pen that is attached to the screen, and you may need some help from Madam Usher. Sir, if you would -- just first of all, if you can locate where your observation point at Kaolin hill was? Just mark that with an X.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if you could circle the areas in which the brigade artillery was located, and just write next to or inside those circles the calibres of the weapons that each of those firing positions possessed. And how many of each of those weapons there were. That would be helpful. Just write it down wherever you can locate where those positions were at the time of the Krivaja-95 operation.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. On this plan I don't see the place where the 122 guns were. I think this is a howitzer position at Repovac in B1 but I don't see Velika Raven. It is some 500 metres to the north where the 122 cannons were. I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Then if you could just first of all mark the first one that you talked about that you can see, and indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we can move the map down, maybe it's further up. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, if you would -- unfortunately this copy is cut off, so we can --

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's just that the witness is being asked to mark gun positions for operation Krivaja-95 but the map he has in front of him is Susica, which was drafted and prepared before. The two don't match. Unless my colleague has a reason for doing so, I'd like to have an explanation for this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a map that has positions indicated. I just want to find out where his guns were placed during this period of time. If they correspond with anything on the map, then so be it. If they don't then so be it. I could show him any map and it wouldn't make a difference. I've made no representations as to what this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, as long as this is made clear we see no problem with proceeding. At the end of the day it's not the purpose for which the map was prepared that counts but the position of the gun posts that he is being asked to mark on it. If, however, this map is not the ideal one in the sense that it is obvious that the witness has in mind also some other spots which are not included in this map, then perhaps we can break now, we can save this one, we can save this one, and if you have a better map that can be uploaded or shown to the witness and which he can mark, then we can proceed after the break, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Gavric, if you would sign your name at the bottom right-hand corner and today's date, which is the 2nd of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your signature and date, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you could write that at the lower right-hand corner, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think now you can have a break, Mr. Gavric. We will call you back in about 30 minutes time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, s'il vous plait.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Very quickly, my colleague has been going with this witness for more than 2 hours he's asked for 3, so I have no problem with the time he is taking. What my question is is rather what is the purpose of the cross-examination of this witness and I'd simply like to know if he is try to get evidence for his own case he should put his case to the witness and say that's my case and that's what I'm going to ask questions to you about. If it's credibility then at least he can tell us so we understand that is he trying to attack the credibility of the witness and I haven't seen any of that so far, and if is he trying to get evidence contrary to what was obtained during examination-in-chief, then that's a different matter. But I just don't see where my colleague is going with his cross-examination. I think it's important that we have a feel for where he is going so that when we get to 3 hours I can say it's enough or it's not enough, thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Thayer, you wish to respond? You know where you are heading?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm following the tune, Mr. President. We -- I think it's quite clear where I've been going with this witness with respect to the shelling of Srebrenica. It took a little while but this is obviously about his credibility when he claims no recollection of the events of 25 May 1995 and recalls solely that there was a tank firing at his artillery position but claims no knowledge and no conduct with respect to these very specific orders and instructions that were being handed down from the Drina Corps in connection with those historic events of the 25th of July. That's all about credibility. And it takes some time to establish through the documents. That is why it is taking the time that it is, Mr. President. With respect to these other areas, this witness was taken through the events of the attack on the Srebrenica enclave. He was asked questions about his conduct during that. He was asked specific questions about whether there was shelling on Srebrenica on Potocari, on the column of refugees who were fleeing from Srebrenica to Potocari. He was asked questions about an encounter with Drago Nikolic on the 15th of July in the morning. These are all areas that I intend to pursue. Obviously most of it, if not all of it, has to do with credibility, Mr. President. And that takes time to work with this witness, in particular, going through these documents and eliciting his responses as to what he recalls about these events at this time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon do you wish to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very quickly, simply to say that at least he should put his case to the witness and tell what is he trying to get from the witness, which he is not doing at the moment, and he is not saying. The witness is repeating his answers that he gave years ago in the previous case when he testified. He is giving the same answers, and he doesn't know why he is being asked again because my colleague is not saying to him you are a liar. If he thinks that witness is a liar, he should put it to him, but is he not doing that. He is not doing anything to the witness, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, let's have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Thayer, let's continue and let's cut it as short as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 2116, please. And this is a different map, and hopefully we can work with the resolution and catch that top part. It's a big document, Mr. Gavric, so it's going to take some time. Now, if we could -- that's it. And perfect. Sir, this is an excerpt from a different map. Does this magnification capture the northward points that you were referring to earlier? Okay. Let's zoom out then.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could see much more on the former map, but I can do it now. I can already locate the -- I can try and locate the position of the pieces. The former map already depicted two of the positions. So whichever way you want me to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we can zoom in, I think it will be easier for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's no problem. I've located the positions and I can draw them on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you've written in "105 2" and something else. Can you just tell us what that says in that circle?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "105 2 pieces."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you've drawn another circle on top of that, what does that say inside, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cannon 122-2 pieces. So this is a firing position and another one behind that firing position.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: B1-5 pieces Repovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what size are those guns, sir, that you've just drawn to the left of the first circle that you drew?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says B1, they were 76 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, if you can just write an X at your observation point on the Kaolin hill?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kaolin hill?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, you've described that location as being just above the DutchBat base; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Overlooking the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you mark where the battalions with their mortars were located?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to do that. I can't draw the firing positions because I did not man those and I'm just aware of the positions where my artillery pieces were. This was the brigade artillery group.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So you've got no recollection as you sit here today as to where those battalion mortar platoons were located during the operation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be pointless for me to draw something that is not correct. I would like to apologise, I have made a mistake about the elevation 438. I would like to annul the X on Ladja and I would like to draw the proper place of the observation point on Kaolin hill. Am I allowed to correct myself and actually draw the correct position of the Kaolin hill observation point?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, do that. Madam Usher will assist you. If you need to cancel anything, you can do that. You can cancel the previous one if you want. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's much better now. It's correct now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's right. And there's a little I think 438 right where you wrote that X, correct, indicating the elevation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one observation point, one elevation. This is the trig point where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you would just sign your name and put today's date October 2nd in the lower right-hand corner and we'll be done with this exhibit. Thank you, sir. We can save it. And we are done. Now, if we may have 65 ter 3025 again briefly. And we'll need to go to page 4 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. Sir, I might have to jump around a little just to save some time so please bear with me. Do you see under "tasks" 6.1.1 in this combat order where it says "open fire on observed targets in the sectors of Potocari school, Pecisica, Budak, Pale and Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just bear with me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Might have to go down, it's at the very bottom of the page, there it is, sir, do you see it?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Next page in B/C/S, please. We can stay where we are in the English. Under 6.2, you referred to this before, the 128 millimetre rocket launcher --

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already discussed this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see where it says at 0300 hours on 6 July 1995 it will fire 4 projectiles, 50 kilometre air bombs on the Potocari sector, the school, the 11 March factory, the Gracac hill, trig point 377, Kula and Orici?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can actually see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, that firing was actually carried out, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know not with these shells as far as I know, but again at 3.00 after that they were supposed to be placed under my command, but as far as I know, the firing never happened and I don't know anything about the 128 launcher. It may be a mistake or an error. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you testified yesterday that the firing didn't occur and at 26506, you said that "This was just an idea, a plan, but it doesn't mean that everything that is planned has to be implemented in the field." I want to show you 233, please. And then I'll put some questions to you. Now, sir, do you see this handwritten combat report from Colonel Blagojevic dated July 6, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: On this handwritten version do you see the reference to firing support against set targets was provided by 70 millimetre shell launcher, school in Potocari, 11 March factory, and wider area of the village of Potocari." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see this, but this is just something that was copied and incorrectly and I can guarantee you that there was no firing in the sector because the no movement of forces had been noticed nor was this an axis of attack either by the Bratunac Brigade or the corps. The axis of attack was on an entirely different side, some 20 kilometres in depth away from Bratunac on an entirely different side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, just so we are clear, your testimony then today is this daily combat report is incorrect? Whoever drafted it got the wrong information and put the wrong information down, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that very often combat reports just followed a pattern and they were drafted by different people, logistics men, infantry men, some of whom did not have the necessary knowledge on writing combat reports. Some just copied things without giving them much thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right, sir. So your testimony is to your knowledge nobody fired at those locations on that time; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my testimony, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me take you back to what you told the Trial Chamber in Blagojevic. When you were shown this daily combat report by Mr. Karnavas, you stated that, and this is at page 8496: "The person who wrote this report should have in paragraph 2 stipulated the fact that fire power support at certain targets was carried out by battalion fire groups and not the artillery brigade because point 2 and point 6 of this combat report are contradictory." So, sir, what you told the Trial Chamber in Blagojevic was that firing happened but it wasn't by the brigade assets, it was by the battalion assets; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, then tell the Trial Chamber what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was that this referred to the infantry battalion. Whoever provided this information was not telling the truth. If there was firing by that part of the 2nd Battalion on my left flank, I would have observed it. But the battalion commander very often did what they did. That's the way things were done.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So we've got somebody lying in the 2nd Battalion; that's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 99 percent, that would be the case. I can even guess who it was, but it doesn't really matter, does it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We don't want you to guess, sir. Let's look at 65 ter 234, please. And with Madam Usher's assistance, I'm going to show you the original because again we have a legibility problem with the e-court version. I'm handing you both the handwritten and the typed version of this document. And if you want to look at the typed written version, that might be a little easier, either way.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you see at paragraph 2 from this 7 July daily combat report from Colonel Blagojevic, it says: "Our forces returned the fire and also fired artillery at the enemy's firing positions"? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraph 6, there's a reference to 30 pieces of 122 millimetre ammo being used. What kind of gun fires that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should say that the brigade artillery group engaged in and 122 millimetre guns actually were -- opened fire on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you about the 11th, I'm asking you about what's clearly stated here on the 7th in this combat report and my question was first of all, what kind of weapon fires the 122 millimetre round? We see 30 pieces being used according to this combat report. What kind of weapon is that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 122 millimetre are fired by howitzers 122 and cannons 122 millimetre as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So my question to you, sir, is was this firing done by any asset of the Bratunac Brigade on 7 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by the Bratunac Brigade, and I wouldn't be able to tell you anything about any other units deployed in any other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me share with you what you told the Blagojevic Trial Chamber about this same daily combat report. And this is at pages 8496 to 8497. Your attention was called to these sections of the report and you stated, and I quote: "The person who was on duty that day and drew up this combat report mixed up the battalion firing group and the brigade artillery, and this is not one and the same thing." Now, sir, I put it to you that in your answers to the Blagojevic Trial Chamber you didn't say anybody was lying, you just said that what was incorrect was that this firing was coming from the brigade battalion firing group and not the brigade artillery. So my question to you is, again, did any Bratunac Brigade assets, be it your mixed artillery group or be it any of the battalion assets fire on 7 July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know the answer would be no. And the only 122 millimetre cannons in the Bratunac Brigade were held by the Bratunac artillery group.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So it's your testimony then, sir, that you had it wrong, you misspoke in the Blagojevic case when you attributed that firing to the Bratunac battalion firing group; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it was wrongly transcribed. And there's just one possibility, that howitzers 122 millimetres were active in some areas, but they did not belong to the brigade but to the 5th Mixed Artillery Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So then are you saying that the operative who drafted this daily combat report got it wrong again when he attributes that 122 millimetre firing to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with full certainty about the Bratunac artillery group, and I really don't know how this was done, how come people just put things on paper in order to meet somebody's expectations or I don't know why, I don't know for what reason would they do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at one more, sir. May we have 65 ter 236, please. And if we may go to the next page in B/C/S, please. And actually, if we can start from I guess the bottom of the previous page in B/C/S. I apologise. Okay, sir, I just want to ask you about some of the usage that's indicated on this report. There's a reference to 700 pieces of bullets, 20/3. What is that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is ammo for an anti-aircraft cannon. I don't know why you would want to tie this with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at a little further down, 200 pieces of 30/2 bullets. What is that? What kind of weapon is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How many, 200? 220? How many? 220, 120, 120 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at the 30/2 reference, it says 200 pieces. I'm just asking you, sir, what is a 30/2? What kind of weapon is that that used those 200 rounds? It's right -- second line from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I think that it was also an anti-aircraft gun but I'm not sure. This is small calibre used in anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at the next entry, it refers to 76 millimetre M18, 60 pieces. What kind of weapon is the 76 millimetre, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a self-propelled gun that uses 76 millimetres as well as B1 cannons and ZIS cannons as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again your testimony, sir, is that no Bratunac Brigade asset discharged a B1 76 millimetre -- I'm sorry, a 70 millimetre round on that day, 9 July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is ammunition that is taken from the logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My question, sir, is, to your knowledge was the -- was an M18 70 millimetre weapon discharged by any asset of the Bratunac Brigade on 9 July 1995, or is this report wrong too?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that because the self-propelled gun was in Pribicevac which is 25 kilometres from where I was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you testified in Blagojevic that from where you were you could see Potocari, and I quote, "extremely well and very precisely." Do you remember saying that? And you stand by that, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of Potocari was placed exactly the same -- exactly that way, I could see it very well since I had the SM61 observation device with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you stand by your testimony in Blagojevic that, and I quote: "Every hit and every projectile fired from our positions was something I could see. That's how it's supposed to be done. You cannot just fire off the top of your head. You have to see where the projectiles fall." That was at 8546 of the transcript. You stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I can clarify it a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you need to, sir. I'm just asking whether you stand by it. Can you answer with a yes or no? If not, you can feel free to explain but I just want to know whether you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my previous answer. I could see that area from my observation post. I can guarantee for that area and not another one which was 30 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you stand by your testimony that not a single round fell near the Muslims walking along the road towards Potocari, and that was at page 8547?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With full moral and other responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with respect to the actual civilians who were fleeing from Srebrenica to Potocari, do you stand by your testimony in Blagojevic at page 8549 that: "All the citizens of Srebrenica who were moving from the direction of Srebrenica towards Bratunac or rather, the industrial zone where they stopped, walked normally, without any panic, at a normal pace, because nobody from our side was disturbing them in any way." Do you stand by that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just to save time, is it fair to say that if I showed you reports from UN military observers and DutchBat and read to you testimony from other UN officers and Muslim civilians about sustained shelling impacting the immediate area of the DutchBat compounds in both Srebrenica and Potocari all through this period from the 6th through the 11th, as well as the shelling tracking the column of refugees fleeing from Srebrenica towards Potocari, that wouldn't change your testimony, would it?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing can change my testimony. I'm telling you what I saw. And I stand by it 100 percent.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked the question in your OTP interview at page 77: "If howitzers were landing on Potocari and Srebrenica, obviously directed as civilian targets could someone else other than you be responsible?" And you answered: "I just told you that on the main axis of the attack which was on the opposite side from me, there were support units and they had two howitzers known as Vozika [phoen] because it's Russian production and it's self-propelled like a tank." Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it exactly but I think something was not interpreted correctly. How can howitzers fire from Srebrenica at people living Srebrenica? I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The interview my colleague is referring to does not appear on the list of documents which were intended to be used by the Prosecution. Neither on the list from yesterday or on today's list so I am a bit surprised to see questions concerning this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, that is a simple oversight, Mr. President, I apologize. I'm sure my friend has the interview of his own witness handy. If he doesn't, I can give him a copy and he can look at it, but I think we can survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Let's proceed. Again try to avoid this recurring as much as you can, please, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked in the interview: "Was any part of your artillery used to drive civilians from one area to another?" And you made a sketch of the UN compounds and you said that, "No one shelled them there, I can guarantee that." Do you recall that, sir? That's at page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Reference please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay, I was just going to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's at page 76 and 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then you were asked: "You weren't responsible for any mortar positions?" And you answered: "No, no, no. Our forces, and I'm talking about 1st and 2nd Battalion, they didn't have a need to fire, they were not in danger. All the offensive came from the direction of Jadar." That's at page 78. Do you recall that testimony, sir, and do you stand by it?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We could not drive away people who were moving towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention now to a different topic, sir. You testified yesterday and that was consistent with your testimony in Blagojevic that the duty officer's assistant when you arrived at the Standard command said that Dragan Obrenovic was asleep because he was tired. Do you remember saying that in Blagojevic at page 8507, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that the duty officer told me that the commander was asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may go into private session for just a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to the encounter that you had on the morning of 15 July with this individual Lukic, let me just read to you what you testified to in Blagojevic. This is at page 8510: "At around 8.30 or 9.00 when I arrived at the entrance gate and the reception area, I met a young man nicely dressed in an all-in-one suit. As far as I knew him, I think he was Lukic. And he tried to talk to me. I was to give him some of my men to go with him on one of his assignments. I refused to do that. And there was a very unfortunate exchange but I don't know what the other man was by rank." And then you say, and this is probably a mistranslation or a problem with the transcript, you say: "He was the security man Drago Nikolic." Actually that may not be incorrect, but your next statement is: "He was the security man Drago Nikolic, he involved himself in our heated conversation and the late Dusko Nikolic, he is deceased today, he was also a school friend of mine, he was killed." Now, my first question, sir, is what if anything did Drago Nikolic say during this encounter?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I need to say that there were many mistakes in that interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you want to correct them, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have to give it, the man asked for it. I think you said I had to or I needed to, whereas I was requested. There's a difference. That's one thing. Another thing, I said that Drago and Dusko Nikolic approached to protect me from the man. They probably saw that it was an ugly conversation which may result in an incident. Dusko Nikolic was killed the next day on the 15th. I didn't say that Dusko was dead at that point in time. As far as I know he was killed on the 16th, not the 15th. That's one thing. Another thing, I know that Drago also intervened but I remember Dusko reacting more vehemently and he addressed the man brusquely. He left and we stayed there talking. I was talking about a handgun and so on. As for Drago, I don't think it was translated correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were asked by Mr. Karnavas same page, 8510: "Let me ask you this, you mentioned Lukic, does he have a first name?" And you answered: "I don't know his first name. I don't know it to this day after all this time. All I know is they referred to him as Lukic. I heard a lot of ugly things about him, bad things about him, and he wasn't at my level. He was a soldier or whatever, but he wasn't in a position to issue any orders to me, let alone me give him my men." And then you were asked: "Where is he from to your knowledge?" And you answered: "As far as I know he was from the surrounding parts of Visegrad." Do you stand by that portion of area tomorrow, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My colleague jumped one line reading from the statement here where it says: "At that time I did not know. Today I do know." He skipped that line. It's very important, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, having heard that, can you tell the Trial Chamber when you learned that he was from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, don't read it the way you did. You should read it all out. It's not nice of you to skip things. I know very well what I said. I said that at that time I didn't know the man. Now I know of him because I heard about him just like many others did. And I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And my question to you, sir, is what did you hear about him?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did I hear? What people were saying, that there was a person from the environs of Visegrad who was with a paramilitary unit. That's all I heard. I have no idea what he was doing, I wasn't with him. It's another matter what I heard from others. It's irrelevant since I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
