utterances.text: And, sir, during the course of these discussions, whatever they were about this Mr. Lukic, it's your testimony that you now believe that this man that you encountered was Lukic from Visegrad, right, that's all I'm try together establish with you. Doesn't matter when you found out, your testimony today is your understanding is this individual who you met on the 15th of July was Lukic from Visegrad; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can only presume that it was Lukic. It may have been Erdemovic as well. He did not introduce himself and no one addressed him. How should I know? I saw him being arrested but I would never have thought that it was the same person I met in Zvornik. I said I supposed it was Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you testified in Blagojevic that you thought of him as a freelancer, someone who goes out to loot. And that's at 8578 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such loose cannons brought only evil. They were only interested in making profit and gains, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to my last area with you, sir. And that's the sweep operation that was conducted on the 17th of July. Can you confirm that this individual Jevic with whom you were working that day went by the nickname of Stalin, that was the nickname that you heard that day?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his nickname was Stalin. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified in Blagojevic that you testified -- sorry, that you ordered the prisoners lined up, and that they lie down with their hands behind their back and ordered their hands tied behind their back. That was at lines 8518 of the transcript. Do you remember that, testifying that you ordered the prisoners to line up and to lie down with their hands behind their back and that you ordered that their hands be tied behind their backs?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, these were not detainees but prisoners. I did order their hands to be tied, although I don't know whether on the back or in the front, but I did order that. That was the natural thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you said that you used twine from raspberry bushes. Was this rope twine or metal wire, sir? Did you understand the question, sir, was that rope twine or was it metal wire?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true we used rope used to bind raspberry bushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And your testimony is that those men were taken by Mr. Jevic and the MUP towards Konjevic Polje; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the operation was finished, I singled out the children from the group. As for the rest of the people who were in the certain age group, they were taken by Jevic who was supposed to take them to Konjevic Polje. There was no sense in taking them to Bratunac and then later on to Bijeljina. I thought it was a good order to give for them to go to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small correction for the transcript. I believe the gentleman mentioned that it was Momir Nikolic who ordered that, I don't see this in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Gavric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said now what I said yesterday, that once the operation was finished I reported to Momir Nikolic who ordered them to be sent to Konjevic Polje rather than to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've been already 2 hours 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is my last section, Mr. President. I'll be able to move through it more quickly I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you saw those prisoners the next day at the warehouse or the hangar in Konjevic Polje where the gas station is now; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that I saw those people in front of a warehouse picking up papers and litter. It wasn't a hangar. It used to be a store and now is a gas station.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked during your interview with the OTP, and this is at page 37 by Dean Manning: "Question: How many men and boys were in that group that you captured?" And your answer was: "My free assessment 35 to 38." And at the Blagojevic trial you were asked how many prisoners were captured on the 17th and you answered: "35 to 38 or rather a total of 38, of those, 3 children and 35 adults, I think." You stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yesterday again you repeated that number 38; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 38 in total including 3 children.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you testified in Blagojevic that they were being guarded by the special police. That was at transcript 8593. Just to clarify, because sometimes that gets translated differently, what did you mean when you said special police guarding those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had in mind the same group that had been with me the day before. It was the deserters that were sometimes referred to as the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you told the OTP at page 33 of your interview that you had information that those prisoners were taken for exchange. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that information was, and from whom you received it?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the children were taken to be exchanged. The rest were supposed to go to Bijeljina to be exchanged for the people from the Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did you know that that was the plan for the adult prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the operation, I remember well, there was much talk about those who surrendered, that they would be exchanged with or for some people from the area of Tuzla and Sarajevo. The place of assembly was supposed to be in Bijeljina, Batkovaca [phoen] or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who gave you that information, sir, who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you. It's a story I heard when we were sitting at the command. Like many, I asked myself what was going to become of those people and then someone from the group said that they were to go to Bijeljina and they would subsequently be exchanged for people from Tuzla and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter 3787, please. Now, the OTP has interviewed the boys who you separated out from the group and who you ended up having filmed; correct? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the OTP interviewed them, I don't know. And it wasn't me who recorded them. I think there was a TV crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that was your idea, sir, was it, to film them, let people know that they were being treated well?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was another reason why I did that, if you want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sure, why don't you share that with us, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We filmed the children so that there would be no news circulating the globe that children were being caught and shot. That was one thing. Another thing, irrespective of the time period, that document can be useful to many in cases such as this one, those children can testify as to their treatment, how I treated them and how they were treated by the rest. It was my idea and that's how we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we interviewed one of those children, sir. Haso Hasanovic in August of 1996 on the 18th of August. He was 16 years old at the time. And if we can go to page 5 of this document. And sir, we'll get the B/C/S up as well. It's going to be the last page of the B/C/S before the witness acknowledgement. It's the last two paragraphs of the interview. Previous page, please. There you go, you've got it. Okay. Sir, he told the investigators about being captured in the area of Burnice. Is that the area where these prisoners were found, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Burnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Apologies for the pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, he spoke of a Serb soldier who said that he wanted to slaughter the prisoners and of another Serb soldier who prevented him from doing that and who appeared to be in charge. That's you; right? We just need an audible answer so we can get it on the --

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. This thing happened when they were arrested and brought to the area of Pervani. One of the volunteers was interested in the children that I separated from the rest. He wanted to liquidate them. That's when I reacted because I really found that a bad thing to do. And I told him nicely that a Serb soldier or officer could not kill anybody old, arrested or under age and that's when I called the police and asked them to arrest him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And actually sir, we need to go to the prior page in the B/C/S, I'm sorry. And where the statement says that the man who was in charge said let the children go, that's you, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we go up a little bit in the statement, when he was talking about what happened during their capture, he said: "We were told to lie down and Serb soldiers moved amongst all of us tying our hands with lengths of wire which had already been cut in preparation." Now, again sir, it's your recollection that that was twine, rope twine, not wire; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was actually not a rope or a rope twine. It was a simple piece of string.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. May we have 65 ter 3786, please. If we can go to page 2 of the B/C/S, please. We also spoke with another one of those boys, Azmir Jusufovic on February 22nd, 2003. This is his statement, his transcript or, sorry, a summary of a phone conversation with him, information report memorializing a conversation on the 19th of February 2002 at 1615 hours. Now, Azmir Jusufovic told us that he was captured in this area of Burnice and taken with other children to the Kaolin factory to the Bratunac Brigade command. Sounds like another one of these children, correct, that you rescued or that you separated?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their names. I ordered Milan Nedeljkovic to put the children in our car for security reasons, and I brought them personally in front of the command of the Bratunac Brigade. I turned them over to the military police and ordered them strictly not to touch them and give them food and this is what I told to Filipovic at the command that they should be covered by the media reports in order to avoid any future situations where people would say that we might have killed these children or ill treated them or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Azmir Jusufovic told the OTP that after they were captured, that is after the group he was with of adult men were captured, he "saw a soldier who had a bundle of approximately 30 to 50 lengths of silver colour wire which were folded in half and were hanging on his belt. He saw the Serb soldiers tying up the hands of Muslim prisoners with such wire." I ask you again, sir, are you sure it was twine and not wire which was used that day to tie up the Muslim prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will kindly ask the witness to remove the earphones in order to propose my objection to the Prosecutor's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make sure that he doesn't understand French. Go ahead, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have allowed my learned friend to ask questions about the first statement referring to the 15th of July. Is there anything, any piece of evidence that the Prosecutor has about the 18th of July to prove that the two young boys were precisely the ones that the witness has referred to so far?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. And before you respond to that, I notice also Mr. Bourgon. Perhaps you will then reply to both of them. Mr. Bourgon. Thank you, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I did not say anything in this line of questioning by the Prosecution, however, I wish to highlight the fact that this is of course the Prosecution at its best in terms of disclosure. These documents that my colleague is using right now were put on the list of exhibits to be used for cross-examination yesterday. The Prosecution has cross-examined this witness years ago in the Blagojevic case and he has described everything about those kids that he says that he saved. Following which the Prosecution at some point in time did some interviews and obtained some material that was not disclosed to us. Was it available, they will say that it was probably available on EDS and those millions and millions of pages on EDS. The situation is on 1 May of this year we indicated that Mr. Gavric here present would be a witness in this case in exactly they know what he was supposed to speak about. They had all the information in order to make this available to us so we could at least at a minimum of decency so that we can show the information to the witness so that he may prepare and explain his story. I think Mr. President, this is a flagrant violation of the rules of disclosure that the Prosecution has. Again they are abusing as they have done throughout this case disclosure, and as a minimum when the witness will retire for the break, I would ask that these documents be given to him so he has a chance to read them because he has never seen them before, these have never been discussed with him. The Defence has never been aware that these documents existed. We have done our homework. We have done what we are supposed to do. We have checked for all documents related to Mr. Gavric, but we did not obtain this information through our search procedure. As a minimum he should be given an opportunity to read this and then I will ask him a few questions in terms of what he did when he saved those children who are still alive today, and what they say in those statements. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Thayer, will you start with Ms. Fauveau's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, these documents were disclosed in the Srebrenica folder of EDS, the specific Srebrenica folder in February of 2006. First of all, we placed these exhibits on our list of cross-examinations yesterday and they were disclosed in that way again yesterday pursuant to the rules that we've been following for the last two years of this trial. I frankly do not understand my friend's argument that there has been some violation here. There has been no violation. We put on our case in chief for two years and abided by the rules that the Trial Chamber had set up. We are now cross-examining witnesses and giving them lists of documents that we intend to use. If my friend thinks that there's anything that he needs to do with these documents, he is free to do that. If either of them want to sit on their redirect or cross, if it happens to be my friends from the Miletic team, they are certainly quite capable of asking this witness any question they want about these documents. This witness has acknowledged and testified about rescuing these children. He has confirmed that it was the area of Burnice. The witness statement that I'm in the process of questioning him about refers to being captured in Burnice, so frankly this objection is absolutely without merit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon, and let's bring it to a close, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My colleague entirely misses the point. They always come back with the same argument that this was put in some kind of Srebrenica folder back in February of 2006. This is always the same thing that they are saying and we have the same argument. There are rules of disclosure and those rules have not been followed. If they know that we are going to call a witness and they have information, information that is against that witness, they have to disclose this to us. This information about three kids that were saved by one of our witnesses, it is entirely incorrect for them, that's the question, they know we are calling the witness, they know what the witness will talk about, they have the information, and they keep it in their back pocket until the witness is on the stand. That's why I say that the Prosecution is abusing the Trial Chamber's order allowing them to wait until cross-examination begins to file -- to give us a list of documents. Because that's when the list is given. They sit there and the minute that they get up for their first question they press on the button and they issue their list by surprise, keeping this in their back pocket. Can my colleague tell me today that how many months he has known about those kids and those documents that he did not give the Defence hoping to take us by surprise? He is not taking us by surprise. He is talking an honest witness and an honest man who came here to testify about three kids that he saved, and now he is being completely taken by surprise with documents that as a minimum he should have had the opportunity to have a look at before so he can explain his story and he can explain the difference. We don't even know if those kids are the same ones that he is referring to. There is no evidence to that other than an area. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we deliberate can either of you read out to us what was the contents of the 65 ter summary that was provided by the Nikolic Defence team to the Prosecution regards to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, Your Honour, I can pull that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you read out the 65 ter summary, Mr. Bourgon, what kind of disclosure duties are you referring to in this case? Normal disclosure or any other special kind of disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the disclosure I'm referring to could be right under Rule 68. Now let me explain to you why it falls under Rule 68. In the Rule 65 ter summary we provided, we say that Gavric testified before the International Tribunal in the Prosecutor versus Blagojevic and Jokic case. In that case when the witness testified, he testified at length about saving those three kids. If the Prosecution has information that can tend to provide information as to what this witness did with those three kids, they cannot hide this information from us until cross-examination time. This witness actually saved those three kids --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Bourgon, if you are referring specifically to Rule 68, in this case we are only possibly dealing with the first two paragraphs thereof, the first one refers to mitigatory or exculpatory material. I don't understand you to be submitting that this is the kind of material in this case. I don't understand it to be your submission. If I'm not correct, please correct me strait away. The other paragraph which is the second one which is without prejudice to the exculpatory disclosure, exculpatory material, the Prosecution shall make available to the Defence in electronic form collections of relevant material held by the Prosecutor together with appropriate computer software with which the Defence can search such collections electronically. So if this is the case I'm just asking you because we are trying to find a solution to this impasse between, but if you could be more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the Prosecution possesses information that confirms that our witness that we will present actually saved three kids, it goes to his credibility. It can affect the way his testimony will be seen by the Trial Chamber, and they ought to give that information to us. Because the information, those statements from the kids, they were obtained by them. I don't know if it was a time when they still wanted him to testify before certain person pleaded guilty, but when they obtained that information, there was a purpose for the Prosecution obtaining this information, obtaining those statements. These have to be disclosed to the Defence if they know about it and if they know we are going to call the witness. They are completely taking us by surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Rule 68 (1) does not include the material which would affect credibility of the Defence evidence. Only Prosecution evidence. So how does it fall under Rule 68 material? It's a disclosure of exhibits to be used during the cross-examination, which should be guided by the guideline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And let's listen also to the summary that you provided and I'll of course give you an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, I can read that summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It was a very short summary. It referred specifically the fact that Gavric testified before the international Tribunal in the Blagojevic case and that he will state that on 17 July, the day that he conducted the sweep operation, that's not written there, he saw in Konjevic Polje area an enormous number of bodies of dead enemy soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just ask my friend to read the summary as it's written, at least the summary I have here which is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are two summaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will read exactly the summary. Gavric testified before the international Tribunal in the Prosecutor versus Blagojevic and Jokic, case number IT-0260. Gavric will provide evidence confirming that Dragan Obrenovic slept at the Zvornik Brigade command during the night between 14 and 15 July 1995. He will also state that on the morning of 15 July 1995, Drago Nikolic was present at the Zvornik Brigade command. Gavric will finally state that on 17 July, he saw in the Konjevic Polje area an enormous number of bodies of dead enemy soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything else before we conclude this debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Proofing notes were disclosed to the Prosecution on 30 September. In these proofing notes we specifically referred to the fact that the witness did not when reading -- when questioned about his testimony in the Blagojevic case indicated to us any material differences from what he testified then to what he will testify the next day. With that information, Mr. President, the Prosecution was fully aware that we would speak about what happened on the 17th of July, the search operation, and those three kids. They obtained specific information for that purpose which must be disclosed to the Defence before their cross-examination start so at least the witness is not taken like this by surprise for something that he did that was good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I still am not clear on your response to Judge Kwon's question, which was, how does this obligation arise under Rule 68 in terms of the provisions of paragraph 1, where is the obligation you're talking about on the Prosecution to disclose to the Defence before their cross-examination starts? Where does that flow from Rule 68 in this instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Judge, I thank you for your question. I mentioned Rule 68 I can build an argument on Rule 68. I prefer maybe to simply put the obligations of the Prosecution on simple decency when they know that we will lead a witness and they take us by surprise by not giving us that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And you are saying there is a different obligation on the Prosecution in cross-examination than there is on the Defence. Because you certainly wouldn't argue that the Defence would have an obligation to disclose that material in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I agree with you, Judge, I think there's definitely, a definite different between what applies to the Prosecution and what applies to the Defence. The basic difference, Judge, that we -- that is very often in our view not being maybe taken into consideration to its right importance is the fact that the Prosecution has a different duty. They have to meet their case beyond a reasonable doubt, they have the burden of proof, and if they have evidence in their possession, they have to disclose that. It is the right of an accused to know the case he has to meet. If I say to the Prosecution, I have a witness, and this witness will come and say something and they have information that will affect that evidence, they have to disclose it to me, if they have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: I have your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Josse, please let's not compound it any further, but please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's exactly what I wanted to hear, Your Honour, really is this: If the ruling impacts only on this witness, then of course we have nothing to add but if this is being blown up into some general discussion about Rule 66 and Rule 68, apropos Defence witnesses and Prosecution obligations, then we do have submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would understand that. Thank you. That brings to an end this discussion. Let me confer one last time with my colleagues. Mr. Thayer, would you like to add anything or I thought you were renouncing to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just again to confirm, that this material was disclosed to the Defence February 22nd, 2006 by Ms. Stewart in an e-mail which attaches a spreadsheet which lists these witnesses' names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have the break now because it's quarter to 6.00, 25 minutes, and after that we'll come back with our decision and then we will continue with the testimony and finish. I want to make sure that you finish this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So to conclude the chapter, having heard your respective submissions and having discussed amongst ourselves, we see the position as either side as follows: Given the circumstances, namely what the circumstances that both of you have described, we do not see that in any case there has been any kind of transgression, violation of the rules of disclosure in this case as regards this witness much so let's proceed. As far as the point raised by Ms. Bourgon, Madam Bourgon, I think -- Madam Fauveau, sorry, my apologies to you, Mr. Bourgon, and to you, Ms. Fauveau. It's not the first time that I have mixed this up. I hope it will be the last. As far as your -- the point raised by you, I think it's a matter of testimony which we will evaluate at the end of the day. If there is no evidence that we are talking of the same individuals, then obviously we are going to discard what deserves to be discarded. Yes, let's continue. And conclude, please. Mr. Bourgon, I'm glad I didn't address you as Mr. Fauveau. Mr. Bourgon, will there be a redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, there will be, Mr. President. I figure about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: About 20 minutes. Okay. Will you conclude, please, Mr. Thayer, thank you, allowing 20 minutes or so for Mr. Bourgon. We've still got till 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll do my best within that 15 minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's see if we still have 3786 on the screen. If we can go to the first page of the B/C/S, please. We can see that Azmir Jusufovic told the OTP that he was captured in Burnice, he recalls that it was in the afternoon hours possibly the 18th of July 1995. And if we go to the second page he indicates that he was taken to the Kaolin factory in Bratunac. Now, sir, as far as you are aware, was there any other group of Muslim children who were rescued by a VRS officer during this day sweep or during this period when you were conducting this sweep and that who were brought to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This boy, Jusufovic, you say that he was 16. At the time he told me he was 14 and that he was from Kasaba near Milici. I remember him well. As for the other two children, they may have been 9 or 10, I think they were two twin brothers. Nice kids. On the 17th in the evening is when I arrived and handed them over to the Bratunac Brigade command. That is what I said a moment ago and I don't know whether there's any need to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't think so, sir. I think we can agree, can we not, that Mr. Ju sufovic was simply off by a day when he told us that it was on the 18th, when I think we can all agree it was on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken on the 18th from the Bratunac Brigade to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What I meant was, the day he was captured, if he said I was captured on the 18th, he is off by a day and we can agree on that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the question I asked you before all the excitement was, he told the OTP that, and I quote: "He saw a soldier who had a bundle of approximately 30 to 50 lengths of silver colour wire which were folded in half and were hanging on his belt. He saw the Serb soldiers tying up the Muslim prisoners with such wire." Again I just want to find out from you sir, does that change your testimony, does it refresh your recollection in any way as to whether it was a string I think as you told us or whether it was wire?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what would needed for me to change it. If it was silver wire, I would say it was rather expensive piece of metal. We did not have that. We had strings that we used to tie the people up.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we can go back to 3787, please. This is the statement of Haso Hasanovic. If we could go to page 5 of the English and that will be the last page of the B/C/S again before the witness acknowledgement. We'll need the prior page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to those paragraphs, could the Prosecutor please determine on what date the boys were taken prisoner? It is the fourth page in the English and I believe the -- towards the end of the statement in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I if I may just continue my cross-examination so I can finish in time. If my friend has any question she thinks need to be asked, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She won't be in a position to ask questions, no, so let's accommodate Madam Fauveau if you can and proceed without major --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm not even sure what the page she is referring to is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of the English version. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, there's reference in this statement to the 15th of July Mr. Hasanovic saying he was captured. As we just talked about with this other boy that you say you knew well, doesn't it sound like he is off by a couple of days in his recollection of the dates? I mean, there's no disagreement, is there, among us that these boys were rescued by you on the 17th of July? There's no doubt in your mind about that date, is there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know if those are the children, the same children that I referred to. I don't know if somebody found some other children in another area. It cannot be on the 15th. I was not in the field then. It is on that day that I returned from Zvornik and was on leave. I was deployed on the 17th, as I've already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, you'll recall, sir, when I asked but this boy just a few minutes ago, Haso Hasanovic, you were quite certain that when he was describing a Serb soldier saving his life from somebody that wanted to slaughter him, that volunteer you spoke about, you had no hesitation identifying yourself as that person; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That child was 9 years old. I quite doubt that his dates are correct. I have some other information. There was another group that I saved and they survived. They told me that they had to undergo special proofings or preparations when approached by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the first page of this statement and date of birth of the boy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is the 16-year-old boy that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- spoke about earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you interviewed him on -- in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He was interviewed in 1996, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, trying my best to finish up in the time, but you just referred to some other group of boys that you rescued that we've never heard about either in your Blagojevic testimony or in any proofing note or anywhere else, so I want to make sure that we are not withholding anything from the Trial Chamber. Why don't you tell us now what you are talking about, because I just asked you whether there was any other group that you were aware of that was rescued from the area of Burnice during this period of time and you said no, so now you are telling us that there was a group. Why don't you tell us about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not children. It was a group that was captured after the Srebrenica operation in Alibegovic, in the area of Srebrenica. I think it comprised five or six people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Right. Now, that was something entirely different, sir. That was in October of 1995 in the southwest area of Srebrenica, Alibegovic, as you said and those were adult males who you drove personally to a place that begins wise a K, and I am afraid I can't remember the name but I'm sure you can tell the Trial Chamber what that place was that you drove the seven adults --

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sokolac Knezina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm not even going to try to pronounce that, sir, but we are not talking about boys there, are we, we are talking about an entirely different group of people from the boys that you rescued on the 17th; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to point that out because it can be of assistance for the Court and perhaps for someone who was accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So just one last time, sir, to your knowledge, there was no other group of young boys or boys of any age other than the ones that you rescued to your knowledge in that area of Burnice during that period of time when you were conducting that sweep that were taken to the Kaolin factory Bratunac command; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I can tell you about the three children only. The next day when the children were supposed to leave, I went to Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, going back, if we can, to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we don't have the witness's complete answer. He said that the next day I went to Sokolac, and he seems to have trailed off, perhaps the witness can repeat what he said after the word "Sokolac".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you complete your answer or repeat it, please, because the interpreters didn't catch up the last part of it. You said the next day when the children were supposed to leave, I went to Sokolac. What else did you say after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I don't know if anyone else had the children. I went to Sokolac. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you look at this page that we have on e-court, from the statement of Mr. Haso Hasanovic, he refers to some people, some other men and young men who he was captured with. He names Sejdalija Oric about 40 years old from Lehovici; Munib Cvrk about 50 years from Brosevci; his son Semir about 18 years also from Brosevci; Ramiz, surname unknown, about 18 years from Bobuljica; his brother Mirso about 22 years old -- 22 years also were there, and Fahrudin Ademovic about 17 years from Susnjari. Now, if we may go into private session for a quick moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, according to the autopsy reports of those individuals, the people that it's the Prosecution's contention are those same people that Mr. Hasanovic listed as being captured at the same time as he was in Burnice, the autopsy reports, and I'll just quickly say for the record P0613 at pages 119 to 122, 127 to 130, 143 to 146, and P615 pages 108 to 112 and 171 to 174, each of these bodies were found with multiple bullets and bullets fragments in their remains in the Cerska mass grave. And my investigation in the last two days took me to an exhumation report by a Dr. Haglund, that's 65 ter 611, and at page Roman numeral (viii), he found that from that mass grave there were a total of 48 wire ligatures recovered from 38 individuals. Sir, my question to you is, having heard this information about these individuals who were captured at Burnice winding up in this mass grave in Cerska, 38 individuals with wire ligatures, does that change your recollection at all about whether these individuals, number one, were tied with twine, with string, or with wire ligatures? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who those people are, if those are the same people. But after they were tied with string, no one probably needed to use any wire. If I understood well, when you were talking about that child's statement, you mentioned that there were some grownups in the prison in the same cell with them, if I understood properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, does this information change your belief at all that the information that you had that those prisoners, those 38 prisoners that you consistently remember being captured in Burnice, that they were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything about those people. I keep saying, as I did in my previous testimony, that I don't know what fate befell those people. All I know is that the children were safe and sound and that they now reside in Tuzla, at least they were there the last time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. After all this excitement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's keep it low key and proceed and conclude because we have to decide what is going to happen tomorrow as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I only have a few questions for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In the period from January to July of 1995 are you aware of orders that were issued to the Bratunac Brigade amongst others not to fire your guns on the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we were forbidden to open any fire at the general area of the Srebrenica enclave. I think it was on the 17th of April 1993, that it happened the last time. On the 18th it was the orthodox Easter and as of that day onwards, it was strictly forbidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, many questions were put to you concerning the 25th of May 1995 by my colleague. I only have one very simple question. To the best of your recollection, when shots were fired in the direction of Srebrenica on that day, was it as a result of incoming fire on friendly forces?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion that a decision was made to return fire because to fire from a tank from a safe area, that is something I cannot comprehend. How come they had a tank there?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have in e-court please, 5D1161. I would like to have page 4 in English. Well, let's start with the first page in both English and B/C/S. Just so you know what this document is, before I turn to the section I want to ask you about, this is a report from the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska, and it is addressed, first of all, to the president of Republika Srpska, but as well as to the command of the corps and we see in the second line Drina Corps. Do you see this, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not with you. I don't know what you are aiming at.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just wanted you to say -- to -- whether you can confirm that this is a report from the Main Staff to, amongst others, the Drina Corps, and that it is dated the 25th of May 1995? And then I will put a question to you on a section of this document.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff sent this to the Drina Corps, he could not send it to a brigade command. It had to follow the chain of subordination with the corps command on the top, and from there orders would come down the line of command to lower units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can turn on this document, please, and have page 4 in English, and page 5 in B/C/S. Sir, I'd like to draw your attention where it says at paragraph 6 of this document, which refers to "in the zone of operations of the Drina Corps." I will read this in English where it says, paragraph (a): "The enemy in the zone of operations of the corps, the focus of enemy activities was on positions of the 1st Birac Infantry Brigade which were attacked by with 82 millimetre mortars. At 10.45 the enemy fired four projectiles on the village of Kiseljak killing a woman. At paragraph (b) it reads: "The situation in the corps, the units responded to enemy fire in a timely manner, targeting the observed targets. All corps units are maintaining the highest level of combat readiness. Artillery fire was opened on the Srebrenica and Gorazde enclaves as well as the Tuzla airport. Units have been placed at the highest level of combat readiness." Sir, does this information which of course would not have been available to you, because it was only sent to the corps, but the operational situation depicted in this document, does that match what you perceive on that day that the Bratunac Brigade responded to enemy fire when those shots were fired on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that matches this what happened on the 20th of May at 7.10 and I told you what happened then and I don't know about the rest, I don't know when it was that an enemy group was infiltrated and killed a soldier in the area of Zargon [phoen] and on the following day or even on the same day there was an ambush in Zeleni, there were four or five of our men were killed, among them was a police officer called Ostra who had been called from retirement. He had been retired before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I'd just like to confirm, at the paragraph I'm referring to, I'm not sure if you have it before you, is 6(b) and at 6(b) it says the units and situation in the corps, the units responded to enemy fire in a timely manner, and then it talks about fire was opened on the Srebrenica. Does that matches your information that when the Bratunac Brigade fired any shells on Srebrenica, it was in response to enemy fire?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only aware of the thing that happened on the 20th of May at 7.10. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I could have in e-court 3358. P3358. Sir, this is a document that was shown to you by my colleague during cross-examination, and it's a document that bears your name and where we see that Colonel Lazic is mentioned. Bearing in mind the questions that were put to you by Mr. Karnavas in the Blagojevic case, bearing in mind the questions that were put to you by myself yesterday, and the questions that were put to you today by the Prosecution, to the best of your recollection, why was the name of Colonel Lazic included on this document?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Lazic must have been at the Bratunac Brigade at the time. That's why his name is mentioned together with the brigade commander's name as a person who had either order us directly or who had alternatively conveyed somebody else's order to return fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know, and I insist on the words know, do you have knowledge, if this Colonel Lazic had any authority to order the Bratunac Brigade to fire on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that particular authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, my colleague put questions to you concerning the locations of your gun positions, one of which was the B1 battery in the Repovac, and you answered that the guns located there were the 76 millimetre guns. My question is the following: This battery position, the soldiers that occupied this position, are those the ones that you picked up on the night of the 14th or the 15th when you travelled by bus from Bratunac to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that part of the unit went down or rather came down and accompanied me to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a soldier by the name of Todor Gavric, and is he one of the soldiers that served on this gun position?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know he was a member of the crew, and his battery commander was Stevo Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, as the chief of artillery in the Bratunac Brigade was it your role to relay the firing orders given to you by your commander or to issue your own orders to fire on your own authority? What was your role as the chief of artillery in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My role was to carry out the orders of the brigade commander to whom I was subordinated. I could give him my proposals but he had the last word. Save for a very exceptional moment when the commander gave me his authority to act in cases of major threats posed against our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. At page 26479, which is yesterday -- well, let me first. My colleague asked you a question about the fact that Obrenovic was sleeping that night, and he asked you a number of questions as to what you stated in the Blagojevic case in this respect. Now, yesterday at page 26479 you stated based on the information received that night, it was your view that Obrenovic was in his office probably resting. Do you have any reason to believe or any information which will allow you to believe that Obrenovic was not resting in his office that night?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he had been anywhere further afield, the duty operations officer would have called him by phone. But since he didn't do that, but physically left the room and go somewhere, I can only suppose that he actually physically went to see Obrenovic and convey my message to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Today you were asked some questions about the encounter with someone who you stated and there were discussions about name Lukic. First, I would like to come back to what you said in the Blagojevic case, and I quote from page 8510 in the transcript. The question was put to you at lines 21: "All right. Do you know where Mr. Lukic was from? Do you know at that point in time?" Answer line 23: "At that time I did not know. Today I do know." Sir, all the questions were put to you yesterday and today, to the best of your recollection is that exactly the situation as it is?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm absolutely certain that I did not know that man. I only supposed and I do still that it was Lukic. However, a lot of people have read a lot of things about this man, Lukic, that he hails from the vicinity of Visegrad, that his brother was killed in an operation to arrest either him or somebody else. That's what I know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One last question on this topic. My colleague read to you part of the transcript on the same page 8510, lines 16 to 17, and the question my colleague read to you was: "All right. Let me ask you this, you mentioned Lukic. Does he have a first name?" Your answer was: "I don't know his first name. I don't know it to this day after all this time. All I know is they referred to him as Lukic." My question is, based on this part of the transcript which was read to you, did at any point in time on the morning of the 15th July 1995 either Dusan Nikolic or Drago Nikolic refer to the first name or the second name of that young man with the one uniform -- one-piece uniform that you met?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday when you questioned me and earlier today when the Prosecutor questioned me, I said it loud and clear, when they came behind me, had they known him, they would have referred to him by his first or last name, Dule would have used his name as they were having that argument. I'm 999 percent sure that they did not know him. How could have they known him? He just turned up there as an individual. They could not know him. They didn't know him, I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I move to the last issue raised by my colleague, which is concerning those kids that you testified about yesterday and today. My first question is, I'd like you to confirm, because I think you said that today, that you did not know and you still do not know their exact names; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I don't know the name. Some family names have been mentioned, but they don't ring any bells. The twins only told me that they were from Karacici, which is a village near Srebrenica and the other blond, an older child told me that he was 14, that he was from Kasaba and that he was an orphan. This is what the children told me and there was no reason for me to double-check their words. Why should I have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, when you -- when this event took place, you mentioned now specifically three kids that were separated and you mentioned what you did about those three kids, but was there any other kid that day, was there a fourth kid that you saved that day, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know. I mentioned three kids. I described how they looked, and these kids, I'm sure, would be able to recognise me. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have in e-court, please, 3786. Sorry, 3787. And in English on page 4 of 9. Now, let me read you a part of what appears before you. I don't think it is available in your language but I will read it to you, and that is at the end of the page -- it's also page 4 in B/C/S. And I read four lines from the bottom of the before-last paragraph: "I did not know the three --" sorry, just a bit higher: "The man who was in charge said to let the children go and he cut the wire that tied my hands behind my back with a knife. The commander then took me to the first bus and I sat in there and found another three kids. I did not know the three, but I talked to one of them and he said he was Hasmir from Nova Kasaba and that he was around 15 years old, and he said that he had been caught an hour ago." Sir, this fourth kid obviously because the three kids are sitting in the bus, this fourth kid, it is possible that it was not you that took this fourth kid or that was there to cut the wire?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, is it possible to cut a piece of wire with a knife? I doubt it. And that child from Nova Kasaba is the child that contacted us, surrendered, he wore a white T-shirt, he was the first one to distance himself from the group, and then returned to the group and asked them to surrender themselves and this is as much as I can remember. I remember the blond kid and I also remember the two twins and I really can't recall a fourth child. As far as I can remember, there were three kids. That's as much as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you at the end, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is it, Mr. President. Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gavric, on behalf of the Trial Chamber I wish you thank you for having come over, on behalf of everyone I also wish you a safe journey back home. You will now be assisted by our staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents? Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't know if the Trial Chamber has received our list of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two documents, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Two documents. The picture 3DIC 224, which the witness marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, this is 5D1 -- [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed Mr. President. I had the wrong number in front of me, it's 5D1161.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objection from anyone. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objections from the other Defence teams? So these two documents are admitted. Now the Borovcanin team had also two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we have two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have the exhibit numbers 4DP00121 and 4DP00255.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from anyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. They are also admitted. Then we have your exhibits, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We've circulated a list. If I can recite them or we can just rely on the list that we've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can rely on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- that we've distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I need to follow line by line because I have objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then we need to do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If it helps in terms of time, we have submissions about this list as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Seems it will take us some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While we get a feedback from the rest of the staff to see whether they are prepared to stay a little bit longer, you've had this list already, Mr. Bourgon, can you indicate to us which ones you are objecting to? Did you follow, Mr. Bourgon? And how long do you think your submission will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President. Maybe if my colleague is ready, I need 5 minutes just to look at the list but it will be very short but I need to look at some of these issues especially those last statements that I need to assess before I can say whether I oppose or not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I can be precise. It's 3786 and 3787 we object to but perhaps before I make my submission, I'd invite my learned friend to explain why he wants them in, for what purpose, because if he is prepared to concede that they are there for a limited purpose then I'm not going to pursue the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. First of all, what is the position with the interpreters and everyone? Okay, we go on a little bit more, but please try to be reasonable and keep your comments as brief as possible. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, our position has been not to introduce the entire statement when a portion is read. Given the excitement that we had about these statements, we would offer them for whatever purpose the Trial Chamber deems appropriate. My friends complained about their alleged late disclosure. If there's any arguments that they want to make, we thought it would be the best practice to give the Court the entire statement. If the Court decides it doesn't want it that's fine. It's absolutely fine with us. It's not our practice to offer the entire statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That doesn't really help a great deal frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me -- give me one minute so that I consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Josse and Mr. Bourgon, it's a bit difficult in the situation because Mr. Thayer utilized portions of the statement in questioning the witness, and those portions will obviously be on the record. If there are suggestions as to the -- the identification of these boys and whether they were the same children, it may be to the advantage of the Defence to have the whole statement in for the purposes of us assessing that whole issue. So but if the Defence is objecting to their admissibility, that would be the purpose for which the Trial Chamber is of the view that those statements in their entirety might be of benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Speaking on behalf the Gvero Defence, Your Honour, we would have no objection to the admissibility of the whole statement on that basis, in other words, if it purely was considered in the context of this witness's evidence. I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Josse and thank you Judge Prost. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to join the objections that have been raised by Mr. Josse. We don't have any objections if these documents are admitted for a limited aim, but as far as the veracity of the statement, I don't think it can be done for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would have never been in our mind in any case. So Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We take the same position, Mr. President, we thank the Trial Chamber, we also agree that the statement should go in in their entirety but for the limited purpose identified by the Trial Chamber. And having looked at the list, although I do have a standing objection that we will put on paper definitely regarding Rule 65 ter and the way that the Prosecution is by the back door introducing a large quantity of new documents and new evidence as part of the Defence case which is entirely contrary to what it should do, Mr. President, other than that we have no objections for the documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we are all admitted. Now, Mr. Bourgon in particular, we received information in the course of the day, actually first thing that reached us this morning that there is some problem, major problem with the witness that you had planned to produce tomorrow against whom a subpoena was issued. My understanding is that the subpoena has been served, but there is a practical problem in that he hasn't -- he is not in possession of a passport as yet. He has applied for one and that it is anticipated that he may be available, probably will be available mid-October or so. Is that information correct to start with?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To begin with, yes, Mr. President that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And having said that, what are your plans? Shall we start -- on Monday of course we'll start with the Borovcanin Defence and you will make arrangements in due course with the Borovcanin Defence to fit in your witness sometime in October or November or whenever you --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are other developments that I wish to inform the Trial Chamber about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But before I do so, I need to put on the record that when the issue came out of this witness obviously we probably did a mistake by not requesting the protective measures along with the subpoena, although we thought that we had implicitly done so by requesting the confidentiality of the subpoena. What I feel important to put on the record today is that I failed to understand the stance taken by the Prosecution concerning the fact that this witness should not be given protective measures and their opposition after I explained to my colleague exactly what the situation of the witness was. Further, to our application the Trial Chamber rendered its decision that it would interview the witness. For the past few days we have been trying to contact the witness, and we did so very recently, very, very recently after he has been issued with a subpoena, we explained to him this interview process and due to his state of mind and for the reasons that I indicated previously to the Trial Chamber, we will be withdrawing the witness, Mr. President. Which puts an end to the case for the Defence of Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bourgon. Would you like to have anything discussed tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, but if we have a couple of more minutes. First I'd like to say that withdrawing the witness implies maybe a request that the subpoena be cancelled, the subpoena that was issued again the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll look at that and we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we had planned to -- we had anticipated to finish earlier today and one thing that we wanted to do at the end the presentation of the case for the Defence is to read out two letters that we've received from witnesses who appeared during our case, two -- one is from the witness 3DW1 which was the Colonel Landry who testified last week and one was witness from the previous week. Both witnesses thought it was absolutely necessary to underscore the outstanding service and the assistance they received while they were here, especially by the victims and witness's section. They were very impressed and they left the Tribunal with a very very good impression. We had statements to read, but due to the time we won't read the statements but we think it's important to pass on the message. They said that they like -- their experience was something that they will remember in a positive sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. And that's pleasant music to our ears. What we will do is if my colleagues agree and I'm sure they will, is that I would ask you to file these letters if you have no problems in doing that, and once they are filed, the registrar is to communicate a copy of the letters to the president of this Tribunal and to the registrar and to the registrar and to the head of the division, victims and witness's division. Thank you Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was about to forget something due to the time, I'm sorry, there are just -- of course this ends the presentation of the case for the Defence of Drago Nikolic. However, that is of course subject to some motions that we still have to file. I indicated that last week. We will be filing these motions. And also one very important issue, and that was that obviously as you saw, Mr. President, the accused did not make a statement at this time. However, it is very likely that he will be requesting to make such a statement at a later time, whether it is part or not part of the case for the Defence. This is something that is still being considered very actively. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll reserve our position on that. Before we conclude, I would like on behalf of the Trial Chamber to thank the -- all the staff, registry, our own staff, the recorders, the interpreters, the technicians and of course all of you present here for having cooperated and overstayed by almost 20 minutes. Thank you very much. We will reconvene on Monday and Mr. Lazarevic, you will start with your Defence case. Thank you.
